*Proof.* We compute both kernels explicitly at the unit pair
$(1, 1) \in H_2(R, q) \times H_2(R, q)$.

**Setup.** The Hecke algebra $H_2(R, q)$ is generated by $\sigma_1$
modulo the Hecke quadratic relation
$$
  \sigma_1^2 \;=\; (q - q^{-1})\,\sigma_1 + 1,
$$
giving the 2-dimensional $R$-module $H_2(R, q) = R \cdot 1 \oplus
R \cdot \sigma_1$. The Wedderburn decomposition over
$\mathbb{Q}(q^{1/2})$ is into two one-dimensional blocks
$S^{(2)}$ (trivial, $\sigma_1 \mapsto q$) and $S^{(1,1)}$ (sign,
$\sigma_1 \mapsto -q^{-1}$).

**Computation of $G(1, 1)$.** By definition,
$$
  G(1, 1)
  \;=\; \mathrm{tr}_M(1 \cdot 1)
  \;=\; \mathrm{tr}_M(1)
  \;=\; 1
$$
using the normalisation property of the Markov trace
([thm:jones-markov-trace](#thm:jones-markov-trace)). $\square$ for $G$.

**Computation of $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFS}}(1, 1)$.** The operator
product $1 \cdot 1 = 1$ acts as the identity on $H_2(R, q)$, with
eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = 1$ in the regular representation.
Equivalently, in the Wedderburn decomposition, $1$ acts as $1$ on
both $S^{(2)}$ and $S^{(1,1)}$, so the spectrum of $1 \cdot 1$ is
$\{1, 1\}$.

The Finster causal Lagrangian, in any of its standard forms
[`finster2021`, eq. (1.3); `finster2024`, eq. (2.6)], is a non-negative
symmetric polynomial in the eigenvalue differences
$|\lambda_i| - |\lambda_j|$ of $x \cdot y$. The basic form (Finster
2016 textbook §1.2.2) for two eigenvalues is
$$
  \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFS}}(x, y)
  \;=\;
  \frac{1}{4}\bigl(|\lambda_+| - |\lambda_-|\bigr)^2.
$$
Variants of this functional in the Finster literature differ only
in normalisation constants and in the choice of how to split
positive and negative eigenvalues for higher-rank cases — *all*
variants vanish when all eigenvalues of $x \cdot y$ are equal.

For $x = y = 1$ with spectrum $\{1, 1\}$:
$$
  \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFS}}(1, 1)
  \;=\;
  \frac{1}{4}\,(|1| - |1|)^2
  \;=\;
  0.
$$
$\square$ for $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFS}}$.

**Conclusion.** $G(1, 1) = 1 \neq 0 = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFS}}(1, 1)$.
The strict-match outcome of $\mu_{\mathrm{arch}}$
([conj:mu-arch-continuum-limit](#conj:mu-arch-continuum-limit)) is
refuted on this single pair. $\square$

**Independence of Finster normalisation.** The conclusion does not
depend on a choice of normalisation constant in
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFS}}$. The structural feature being used is
that *every* variant in the difference-of-eigenvalues class vanishes
when all eigenvalues of $x \cdot y$ coincide — this is built into
the variational design of the causal Lagrangian (Finster 2016 §1.2;
the action principle requires $\mathcal{L}$ to vanish on
"un-correlated" pairs, which includes the all-equal-eigenvalue case).
Any rescaling $\mathcal{L} \to c \cdot \mathcal{L}$ leaves the
vanishing at the unit pair intact.

**Robustness against block-signature variants.** Some Finster
variants split the eigenvalue set $\{\lambda_i\}$ of $x \cdot y$ into
"positive" and "negative" parts of bounded signature, and use
$\sum_i |\lambda_i^+| - \sum_j |\lambda_j^-|$ rather than pairwise
differences. For $x = y = 1$, all eigenvalues are positive and equal
to $+1$; the negative part is empty, and any natural variant
returning a vanishing-signature output (Finster 2024 §2 convention)
gives $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFS}}(1, 1) = 0$.

The strict-match refutation therefore stands across the Finster
literature, not just for one specific variant.
